name: VPNs and IPsec
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Explain how site-to-site and remote access VPNs protect traffic, what IPsec, IKE, ESP and AH do, and why GRE rides over IPsec.

lesson.intro: The internet is cheap and everywhere, but anyone along the path can read or change your packets. A VPN builds a protected tunnel across it, so two offices, or a laptop and an office, can talk as if they shared a private network.
objectives: Explain the four VPN goals and the cryptography that provides them
Compare site-to-site and remote access VPNs
Describe IKE, security associations, ESP, AH, tunnel mode and transport mode
Explain GRE over IPsec, overlay and underlay
Read IPsec tunnel status and choose a VPN for a scenario

sections.title: Why VPNs: a private network over the internet
sections.key: A VPN wraps each packet in a new one between two gateways and adds confidentiality, integrity, authentication and anti-replay; a tunnel by itself is only encapsulation.
sections.body:
A company has a headquarters and twelve branches. Private WAN circuits are expensive; business internet is cheap and everywhere. But on the internet, packets cross networks you do not control, where they can be read, copied or changed.

A **virtual private network (VPN)** builds a **tunnel**. A **VPN gateway** (or headend) protects the original packet and wraps it in a new packet with public addresses, which internet routers use to forward it. The far gateway unwraps and checks it, then forwards the original.

[[visual]]

A secure VPN delivers four things:

[[visual 2]]

A tunnel alone only means encapsulation. Some tunnels, like plain GRE, encrypt nothing.

visual.title: Before and after the branch gateway
visual.caption: Top: the packet PC 10.2.2.2 sends. Bottom: what crosses the internet. Routers on the path see only the new outer header.

visual.title: The four goals
rows: Anyone who captures the packet sees only encrypted data
Any change to the packet in transit is detected
Each end verifies the other is the expected peer, not an impostor
Copied packets cannot be resent later and accepted

sections.pitfall: Assuming every tunnel is encrypted. Tunnel means encapsulation; GRE tunnels, for example, carry traffic in the clear unless IPsec is added.

activity.title: Encapsulation, one more time
activity.prompt: Step through the journey and watch each layer wrap the one above it, then get unwrapped at the far end. A VPN gateway adds one more wrapper: it encrypts the whole IP packet and puts a new IP header (with public addresses) in front. Ask yourself which header the internet routers read once the packet is inside the tunnel.

check.question: An attacker records valid packets from a VPN session and sends them again later, hoping the receiver accepts them. Which VPN goal defeats this?
choices: Confidentiality
Anti-replay
Data integrity
Authentication
check.explanation: Anti-replay protection tracks sequence numbers and rejects packets it has already seen. The replayed packets are unchanged, so integrity checks alone would pass them.

sections.title: Cryptography building blocks
sections.key: VPNs use asymmetric keys and certificates to authenticate peers, Diffie-Hellman to agree on keys, fast symmetric AES for the data and an HMAC for integrity.
sections.body:
Every secure protocol in this domain (IPsec, TLS, SSH, WPA3) is built from the same few parts.

[[visual]]

**Symmetric encryption** uses one shared key and is fast, so it carries the bulk data. **Asymmetric** cryptography uses a **public key** anyone may know and a **private key** that never leaves its owner. It is far slower, so it is used only to authenticate and set up keys.

A plain **hash** proves nothing about who sent the data, because anyone can compute it. An **HMAC** mixes in a secret key, so only a key holder can produce it. A **certificate**, signed by a **certificate authority (CA)** you trust, binds a name to a public key. CAs, certificates and revocation lists form a **public key infrastructure (PKI)**.

visual.title: Building blocks
rows: A fixed-size fingerprint; one changed bit changes it completely, and it cannot be reversed
Integrity plus proof the sender holds the key
A hash processed with a private key
Proof of who signed and that nothing changed
A shared secret that is never sent
A trusted binding of a name to a public key

sections.pitfall: Thinking public key encryption protects the bulk data in a VPN. It is far too slow; it authenticates the peers and helps set up keys, and AES carries the data.

check.question: Why do IPsec and TLS use asymmetric cryptography only during setup and AES for the data itself?
choices: Asymmetric algorithms cannot encrypt data at all
Symmetric encryption is far faster, so it suits bulk traffic, while asymmetric keys solve authentication and key exchange
AES does not need any key
Every peer shares the same private key
check.explanation: Public key operations are expensive, so they are used where they are uniquely useful: proving identity and helping set up keys. The bulk traffic then uses a fast symmetric cipher with the agreed keys.

sections.title: Site-to-site VPNs
sections.key: A site-to-site VPN is a permanent tunnel between two gateways that protects every host at both sites, and the hosts never know it exists.
sections.body:
A **site-to-site VPN** connects whole networks. Engineers configure a VPN gateway (router or firewall) at each site, and the tunnel between their public addresses stays up permanently. The hosts need nothing installed:

[[visual]]

Any internet access works underneath (fiber, cable, DSL, 4G or 5G), so it is a cheap replacement or backup for private WAN links. The CCNA associates site-to-site VPNs with **IPsec**. With many sites, the tunnel count matters:

[[visual 2]]

An **MPLS VPN** bought from a carrier is different: it keeps each customer's routes and traffic separate, but encrypts nothing by default, so you trust the carrier. IPsec trusts nobody on the path, which is why some companies run IPsec on top of MPLS.

messages.label: Normal packet to 10.1.1.1
messages.detail: PC1 knows nothing about the VPN

messages.note: Internet routers forward on the outer header and see only ciphertext

visual.title: Tunnels for n sites
rows: Branch-to-branch traffic detours through the hub
Direct paths, but the count grows fast
Hub tunnels permanent, spoke-to-spoke built on demand

sections.pitfall: Thinking every branch PC needs VPN client software for a site-to-site VPN. Only the two gateways are configured; the hosts send ordinary packets.

check.question: In a site-to-site IPsec VPN between two offices, which devices need VPN configuration?
choices: Every PC and server at both sites
Only the PCs that access the other site
The ISP routers along the internet path
Only the VPN gateways, such as the two edge routers or firewalls
check.explanation: Site-to-site VPNs are built between gateways. Hosts send normal packets, and the gateways encrypt and decrypt on their behalf. The ISP simply routes the outer packets.

sections.title: What IPsec provides, and how
sections.key: IPsec is a framework: AES for confidentiality, an HMAC for integrity, a pre-shared key or certificates for authentication, sequence numbers for anti-replay, Diffie-Hellman for keys.
sections.body:
**IPsec** (RFC 4301) is not one protocol but a framework. It says how two peers reach the four VPN goals and lets them choose an algorithm for each, so when one weakens, they agree on a better one.

[[visual]]

How do two routers agree on a secret key across an internet they do not trust? **Diffie-Hellman (DH)**: each side combines exchanged public values with its own private value, and both compute the same secret, which never crosses the wire. An eavesdropper who sees the whole exchange still cannot compute it.

DH comes in numbered **groups**: 1, 2 and 5 are too weak today, and group 14 (2048-bit) or an elliptic curve group is the usual minimum.

visual.title: How IPsec meets each goal
rows: Both peers hold the same session key
The receiver recomputes it; one changed bit and the packet is dropped
Certificates scale better: no secret to share with every peer
A sequence number in every packet
Duplicates and very old numbers are dropped
A shared secret that never crosses the network

sections.pitfall: Mixing up integrity and confidentiality. A hash like SHA-256 proves the data was not altered, but the data is still readable unless it is also encrypted.

check.question: What problem does Diffie-Hellman solve for two IPsec peers?
choices: It lets them derive the same secret key without ever sending the key across the network
It encrypts every data packet in the tunnel
It proves that each packet arrived unchanged
It assigns private IP addresses to remote users
check.explanation: Diffie-Hellman is a key agreement method: both sides compute the same shared secret from exchanged public values. The bulk encryption itself is done by a symmetric cipher such as AES.

sections.title: IKE: building the tunnel
sections.key: IKE (UDP 500, or 4500 through NAT) builds the tunnel: phase 1 creates a protected IKE SA, then phase 2 builds two one-way IPsec SAs for the data.
sections.body:
IPsec works in two stages: negotiate, then protect data. Negotiation starts when **interesting traffic** (a packet matching the VPN policy) reaches a gateway with no tunnel yet.

**IKE (Internet Key Exchange)** negotiates on **UDP 500**, moving to **UDP 4500** when NAT is detected (**NAT traversal**, NAT-T). It authenticates the peers, agrees on algorithms, runs Diffie-Hellman and builds **security associations (SAs)**. An IPsec SA is a one-way agreement on keys, algorithms and lifetime; each packet's **security parameter index (SPI)** names its SA.

[[visual]]

**IKEv2** does the same job with fewer messages, built-in NAT traversal and better remote access support. SAs expire and are renegotiated with fresh keys automatically.

steps.label: Interesting traffic arrives
steps.detail: The router contacts the peer on UDP 500

steps.label: Phase 1: agree, run DH, authenticate
steps.detail: Policies must match (encryption, hash, PSK or certificates, DH group, lifetime); a mismatch or wrong PSK stops everything

steps.label: The IKE (ISAKMP) SA is up
steps.detail: A protected two-way channel for the rest of the negotiation

steps.label: Phase 2: build the IPsec SAs
steps.detail: Inside the IKE SA: a matching transform set (ESP, AES, SHA-256) and the traffic to protect; two SAs, one per direction

steps.label: User data flows as ESP
steps.detail: IP protocol 50, or inside UDP 4500 with NAT-T

sections.pitfall: Troubleshooting phase 2 when phase 1 never came up. Phase 2 runs inside the phase 1 channel, so a mismatched pre-shared key or policy stops everything; always check phase 1 first.

check.question: Two routers are configured for a site-to-site IPsec VPN, but their pre-shared keys do not match. What happens?
choices: Phase 1 fails, so no IPsec SAs are built and no traffic is protected
Phase 1 succeeds but phase 2 fails
The tunnel comes up without encryption
The routers fall back to a plain GRE tunnel
check.explanation: The pre-shared key authenticates the peers in phase 1. When authentication fails, the IKE SA never forms, and phase 2 has no protected channel to run in, so no IPsec SAs exist at all.

sections.title: ESP, AH, tunnel mode and transport mode
sections.key: ESP (IP protocol 50) encrypts and authenticates; AH (51) only authenticates and fails through NAT. Tunnel mode wraps the whole packet; transport mode protects only its payload.
sections.body:
Once the SAs exist, one of two IPsec protocols protects user data. Both sit directly on IP with their own protocol numbers, not on TCP or UDP.

[[visual]]

**Tunnel mode** encrypts the whole original packet, header included, and adds a new IP header with the gateways' addresses: what site-to-site gateways need. **Transport mode** keeps the original header and protects what follows, which suits host-to-host traffic and GRE over IPsec.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

ESP adds a trailer (padding for the cipher's block size) and an **integrity check value (ICV)**. Its header carries the sequence number that anti-replay checks.

visual.title: ESP and AH
rows: Yes, including the outer IP header
No: NAT's address rewrite fails the check

visual.title: ESP transport mode
visual.caption: The ICV covers the ESP header, the encrypted part and the trailer.

sections.pitfall: Believing AH encrypts because it is part of IPsec. AH only authenticates; if a question requires confidentiality, the answer is ESP.

check.question: Which IPsec protocol provides confidentiality by encrypting the payload?
choices: AH
IKE
ESP
GRE
check.explanation: ESP (IP protocol 50) encrypts and authenticates. AH authenticates without encrypting, IKE only negotiates keys and SAs, and GRE is an unencrypted tunneling protocol.

sections.title: Remote access VPNs
sections.key: A remote access VPN is an on-demand tunnel from one device, usually TLS on port 443 from a client such as Cisco Secure Client (formerly AnyConnect).
sections.body:
A sales engineer on hotel Wi-Fi needs internal apps, and hotel networks are where a man in the middle lurks. A **remote access VPN** lets the laptop build its own tunnel to a **headend** (a firewall or router) on demand, using client software such as **Cisco AnyConnect**, now **Cisco Secure Client**.

The CCNA associates remote access with **TLS** on TCP 443, which almost every hotel firewall allows. Clients add **DTLS** on UDP 443, because TCP inside a TCP tunnel stalls voice and video when packets are lost. IPsec with IKEv2 also works.

[[visual]]

A **clientless** VPN needs only a browser: a TLS portal reaches web apps. A **full tunnel** sends all traffic to headquarters; a **split tunnel** sends only company traffic.

[[visual 2]]

messages.label: Certificate
messages.detail: proves it is the real gateway

messages.label: Inner IP from the VPN pool

visual.title: Remote access or site-to-site
rows: On demand: the user starts it

sections.pitfall: Equating any HTTPS website with a client VPN. A browser's TLS session protects that one session only; a client VPN carries all of the device's enterprise traffic through one protected tunnel.

check.question: Which protocol does the CCNA associate with remote access VPN clients such as Cisco AnyConnect?
choices: TLS
GRE
AH
PPP
check.explanation: Remote access client VPNs typically use TLS, often on port 443 so they pass through public firewalls. IPsec is the typical site-to-site protocol, and GRE and AH provide no encryption.

sections.title: GRE over IPsec, tunnels and overlays
sections.key: GRE (IP protocol 47) carries multicast and routing protocols through a tunnel interface but encrypts nothing, so GRE over IPsec combines its flexibility with IPsec protection.
sections.body:
Two offices share a classic IPsec tunnel, and OSPF will not form a neighbor across it: classic IPsec protects matching unicast traffic, and OSPF hellos are multicast (224.0.0.5).

**GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation, IP protocol 47)** creates a virtual point-to-point **tunnel interface**. Anything routed into it, including multicast, broadcast and non-IP traffic, is wrapped in GRE plus a new IP header, so routing protocols work as on a serial link. But GRE has **no encryption, integrity or authentication**.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

The internet underneath is the **underlay**; the tunnels on top, with their own addressing and routing, form the **overlay**. SD-WAN and SD-Access (VXLAN) reuse the idea.
sections.code:
interface Tunnel0
 ip address 172.16.0.1 255.255.255.252
 ! Underlay: our public interface and the far router's public address
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/0
 tunnel destination 128.107.1.1
 ! Encrypt the GRE packets with IPsec
 tunnel protection ipsec profile VPN-PROFILE
!
router ospf 1
 ! OSPF neighbors form across the tunnel (overlay)
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
sections.deeper:
**Checking a GRE tunnel.** `show interfaces tunnel 0` shows whether the tunnel is up/up, its source and destination, and `Tunnel protocol/transport GRE/IP`. Do not trust up/up alone: without keepalives, a GRE tunnel interface stays up as long as the router has a route to the tunnel destination, even if the far end is not configured. A ping across the tunnel is the real test.

**DMVPN** builds on the same GRE plus IPsec idea, but creates spoke-to-spoke tunnels dynamically instead of configuring every pair by hand.
sections.pitfall: Assuming a GRE tunnel is a VPN in the secure sense. Without IPsec, anyone on the path can read and change everything inside it.

check.question: Why do engineers often run GRE inside IPsec instead of using IPsec alone between two sites?
choices: GRE adds the encryption that IPsec lacks
GRE carries multicast and routing protocol traffic such as OSPF, which a classic IPsec tunnel does not
GRE makes the tunnel faster by compressing packets
IPsec cannot cross the internet without GRE
check.explanation: GRE provides a tunnel interface that carries multicast, so routing protocols work; IPsec then provides the security GRE lacks. GRE itself encrypts nothing.

sections.title: Verifying a tunnel and choosing the right VPN
sections.key: In `show crypto isakmp sa`, QM_IDLE means phase 1 is up and MM_NO_STATE means it failed; `show crypto ipsec sa` counters show protected traffic each way.
sections.body:
The CCNA does not ask you to configure IPsec, but reading a tunnel's state is a likely exhibit.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

Between the peers, edge ACLs must permit **UDP 500** (IKE), **ESP** (IP protocol 50) and **UDP 4500** (NAT traversal).

Choosing a VPN comes down to who needs access, and from where:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Reading the output
rows: Phase 1 is complete: the IKE SA is up and ready
Peer reachable on UDP 500 or 4500? Policies and pre-shared keys match?
This side sends; nothing protected comes back
The peer's routing and crypto policy, or a filter dropping ESP
Traffic is not matching the crypto policy
Which subnets the VPN is set to protect

visual.title: Which VPN?
rows: Whole sites that talk all the time
Site-to-site IPsec; GRE over IPsec or DMVPN when routing protocols must cross
A remote access VPN client, TLS or IKEv2
A contractor needs one web app from an unmanaged PC
A carrier MPLS WAN that must also be encrypted
IPsec on top of the MPLS VPN

sections.code:
R1# show crypto isakmp sa
IPv4 Crypto ISAKMP SA
dst             src             state          conn-id status
128.107.1.1     64.100.9.9      QM_IDLE           1001 ACTIVE

R1# show crypto ipsec sa
! lines omitted
   local  ident (addr/mask/prot/port): (10.2.2.0/255.255.255.0/0/0)
   remote ident (addr/mask/prot/port): (10.1.1.0/255.255.255.0/0/0)
   current_peer 128.107.1.1 port 500
    #pkts encaps: 1205, #pkts encrypt: 1205, #pkts digest: 1205
    #pkts decaps: 1198, #pkts decrypt: 1198, #pkts verify: 1198
sections.deeper:
**Counters.** `#pkts encaps` and `#pkts encrypt` count packets this router protected and sent into the tunnel; `#pkts decaps` and `#pkts decrypt` count protected packets it received and opened. Any counters at all on an IPsec SA mean phase 2 succeeded.

**GRE over IPsec through an ACL.** The GRE packets travel inside ESP, so protocol 47 never appears between the peers; only UDP 500, ESP and UDP 4500 do.
sections.pitfall: Reading QM_IDLE as a problem because it says idle. It is the healthy phase 1 state; MM_NO_STATE is the one that means phase 1 failed.

check.question: show crypto isakmp sa lists the peer with the state QM_IDLE. What does that mean?
choices: Phase 1 failed and is waiting to retry
IKE phase 1 is complete and the IKE SA is up and ready
No traffic matches the crypto policy
The peer skipped authentication
check.explanation: QM_IDLE is the healthy phase 1 state: the IKE SA exists and is idle until quick mode (phase 2) is needed again. MM_NO_STATE is the state that points to a phase 1 failure.

keyTerms.definition: A secure tunnel across an untrusted network that provides confidentiality, integrity, authentication and anti-replay.
A permanent VPN between gateways at two sites that protects traffic for every device at both sites; usually IPsec.
An on-demand VPN from one device's client software to an enterprise headend; usually TLS.
A framework of protocols (IKE, ESP, AH) that secures IP traffic with a choice of algorithms for each security goal.
Internet Key Exchange: authenticates IPsec peers, negotiates algorithms and builds security associations over UDP 500 (4500 with NAT-T).
Encapsulating Security Payload, IP protocol 50: provides encryption, integrity, authentication and anti-replay.
Authentication Header, IP protocol 51: provides integrity and authentication but no encryption, and does not work through NAT.
A key agreement method that lets two peers compute the same secret key without sending it over the network.
IPsec mode that encrypts the whole original packet and adds a new IP header; used by site-to-site gateways.
Generic Routing Encapsulation, IP protocol 47: a tunnel that carries multicast and routing protocols but provides no security.
Encryption that uses one shared key in both directions; fast enough for bulk data. AES is the standard.
A trusted party that signs certificates binding names to public keys, so peers can authenticate without sharing secrets.
A hash computed with a secret key, giving integrity plus proof that the sender holds the key.
A one-way agreement on keys, algorithms and lifetime between IPsec peers, identified by an SPI.
Wrapping IKE and ESP in UDP 4500 so IPsec works through NAT devices.
IPsec mode that keeps the original IP header and protects only the payload; used host to host and for GRE over IPsec.
Remote access VPN design where only traffic for company subnets uses the tunnel and the rest goes straight to the internet.

summary: A VPN tunnels packets across an untrusted network with confidentiality, integrity, authentication and anti-replay.
Certificates or PSKs authenticate, Diffie-Hellman agrees on keys, AES encrypts and HMACs detect changes.
Site-to-site: permanent IPsec between gateways, invisible to hosts. MPLS VPNs separate traffic but do not encrypt.
IKE (UDP 500, 4500 with NAT-T) builds the IKE SA, then two IPsec SAs; ESP (50) encrypts, AH (51) does not.
Remote access: on demand from one device, usually TLS. GRE (47) carries routing protocols but needs IPsec.
QM_IDLE is a healthy phase 1; MM_NO_STATE means phase 1 failed.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a branch manager how a packet from a branch PC reaches a headquarters server safely across the internet through a site-to-site IPsec VPN, naming what IKE phase 1, phase 2, ESP and Diffie-Hellman each contribute, then explain how this differs from a salesperson's remote access VPN from a hotel and from the company's MPLS VPN.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a VPN?
choices: To increase the bandwidth of an internet connection
To assign private IP addresses to remote users
To carry traffic securely across an untrusted network such as the internet
To replace routing protocols between sites
questions.explanation: A VPN builds a protected tunnel so traffic can cross an untrusted network with confidentiality, integrity, authentication and anti-replay.

questions.question: Match each VPN security goal to what it guarantees.

pairs.right: Someone who captures the packet cannot read it
Any change to the packet in transit is detected
The far end is the expected peer, not an impostor
Copied packets cannot be resent later and accepted

questions.explanation: These are the four goals Cisco lists for VPNs. Encryption provides confidentiality, HMACs provide integrity, PSKs or certificates authenticate peers, and sequence numbers stop replays.

questions.question: A packet travels through a site-to-site IPsec tunnel in tunnel mode. Which addresses do internet routers use to forward it?
choices: The original private source and destination addresses
The public addresses of the two VPN gateways in the new outer IP header
The MAC addresses of the two VPN gateways
The addresses inside the ESP trailer
questions.explanation: In tunnel mode the original packet is encrypted and a new IP header with the gateways' public addresses is added. Internet routers only see and route on that outer header.

questions.question: Which statement describes a site-to-site VPN?
choices: A permanent tunnel between gateways that protects traffic for all devices at both sites
An on-demand tunnel started by one user's laptop
A browser session to a single secure website
A private leased line from a service provider
questions.explanation: Site-to-site VPNs connect networks through gateways and stay up all the time. On-demand tunnels from a single laptop are remote access VPNs.

questions.question: Put the steps in order for a branch PC sending a packet to a headquarters server over a site-to-site IPsec VPN.
items: The PC sends a normal packet addressed to the server's private IP
The branch router encrypts the packet and adds ESP and a new public IP header
Internet routers forward the packet using the outer public addresses
The headquarters gateway verifies integrity and the sender, then decrypts
The server receives the original packet from the PC
questions.explanation: The host is unaware of the VPN. The gateways do all the protecting and unprotecting, and the internet only sees the outer header.

questions.question: A new branch joins the company's site-to-site VPN. What must be installed on the branch's 40 PCs so they can reach headquarters securely?
choices: The Cisco Secure Client on every PC
A digital certificate on every PC
Nothing; the branch gateway protects their traffic
A GRE tunnel interface on every PC
questions.explanation: In a site-to-site VPN the gateways encrypt and decrypt for everyone behind them. The PCs send ordinary packets and need no VPN software.

questions.question: Which IPsec mechanism lets the receiver detect that a packet was modified in transit?
choices: AES encryption
Diffie-Hellman key exchange
An HMAC such as HMAC-SHA-256
NAT traversal
questions.explanation: A keyed hash computed over the packet changes if any bit changes, so the receiver drops altered packets. AES hides data but integrity is the job of the HMAC.

questions.question: Two IPsec peers have never communicated before and share no session key. How do they end up with the same secret key without an eavesdropper on the internet learning it?
choices: One peer sends the key in clear text inside the first IKE message
They use Diffie-Hellman, combining exchanged public values with their own private values
They hash their IP addresses with SHA-256
The certificate authority emails the key to both peers
questions.explanation: Diffie-Hellman lets both sides compute the same shared secret from public values plus private values that never leave each device. Watching the exchange is not enough to compute the secret.

questions.question: Which algorithm provides the confidentiality in a modern IPsec VPN?
choices: SHA-256
Diffie-Hellman group 14
RSA signatures
AES
questions.explanation: AES is the symmetric cipher that encrypts the data. SHA-256 provides integrity, Diffie-Hellman agrees on keys and RSA signatures authenticate peers.

questions.question: Which two methods can IPsec peers use to authenticate each other? (Choose two.)
choices: A pre-shared key configured on both peers
Digital certificates signed by a trusted CA
Matching OSPF router IDs
Comparing MAC addresses
A shared SNMP community string
questions.explanation: IPsec peers authenticate with a pre-shared key or with certificates (RSA signatures). Certificates scale better because no secret must be shared with every peer.

questions.question: ESP is carried directly over IP. What is its IP protocol number?
questions.explanation: ESP is IP protocol 50 and AH is IP protocol 51. Neither uses TCP or UDP ports, unless NAT traversal wraps ESP in UDP 4500.

questions.question: A security policy requires that VPN traffic be unreadable to eavesdroppers. Why would an engineer reject a design that uses only AH?
choices: AH does not encrypt the payload
AH cannot authenticate the peer
AH has no anti-replay protection
AH only works over TCP
questions.explanation: AH provides integrity, authentication and anti-replay but no encryption, so the data stays readable. ESP is needed for confidentiality.

questions.question: A tunnel configured to use AH fails whenever the branch router sits behind the ISP's NAT device, while ESP works. Why?
choices: NAT devices block IP protocol 50 but allow 51
AH protects the outer IP header, so NAT's address rewrite makes every integrity check fail
AH requires multicast, which NAT cannot translate
NAT encrypts AH packets a second time
questions.explanation: AH's integrity check covers the outer IP addresses. When NAT rewrites the source address, the receiver's check fails. ESP does not protect the outer header and can be wrapped in UDP 4500 for NAT traversal.

questions.question: Match each protocol to the number it uses on the wire.

pairs.left: IKE and ESP with NAT traversal

questions.explanation: ESP, AH and GRE sit directly on IP with protocol numbers. IKE uses UDP 500, and when NAT is detected, IKE and the ESP traffic move to UDP 4500.

questions.question: What is the difference between IPsec tunnel mode and transport mode?
choices: Tunnel mode encrypts only the payload; transport mode encrypts the whole packet
Tunnel mode uses AH; transport mode uses ESP
Tunnel mode encrypts the whole original packet and adds a new IP header; transport mode keeps the original header and protects the payload
Tunnel mode is for remote access; transport mode is for site-to-site
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode hides the original addresses inside the encrypted part, which is what site-to-site gateways need. Transport mode keeps the original header, which suits host-to-host use and GRE over IPsec.

questions.question: In IKEv1, what is the purpose of phase 2?
choices: To discover the peer's MAC address
To negotiate the IPsec security associations that protect user data
To build the GRE tunnel interface
To elect a designated VPN gateway
questions.explanation: Phase 1 builds a protected channel for the negotiation itself; phase 2, inside that channel, negotiates the IPsec SAs (one per direction) used for user traffic.

questions.question: The HQ router filters inbound internet traffic with the ACL below. The branch router (public address 64.100.9.9) now sits behind its ISP's NAT device, and the tunnel will no longer come up. What must be added?
questions.code:
ip access-list extended OUTSIDE-IN
 permit udp host 64.100.9.9 host 128.107.1.1 eq isakmp
 permit esp host 64.100.9.9 host 128.107.1.1
 deny   ip any any log
choices: permit ahp host 64.100.9.9 host 128.107.1.1
permit gre host 64.100.9.9 host 128.107.1.1
permit tcp host 64.100.9.9 host 128.107.1.1 eq 443
permit udp host 64.100.9.9 host 128.107.1.1 eq 4500
questions.explanation: With NAT in the path, NAT traversal moves IKE and the ESP traffic into UDP 4500, which the ACL denies. isakmp is UDP 500, already permitted. AH would not work through NAT anyway.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a remote access VPN?
choices: A permanent tunnel between two branch routers
An on-demand tunnel from one user's device to the enterprise
A tunnel that only carries routing protocol updates
A private WAN circuit leased from a carrier
questions.explanation: Remote access VPNs protect one device and are started when the user needs them. Permanent gateway-to-gateway tunnels are site-to-site.

questions.question: Why does running remote access VPNs over TLS on port 443 help travelers?
choices: Port 443 traffic is faster than other ports
TLS does not need any authentication
Hotels and coffee shops almost always allow port 443 through their firewalls
TLS automatically assigns a public IP to the laptop
questions.explanation: Port 443 is the HTTPS port, so public networks rarely block it. A VPN using IPsec ports or protocol 50 is more likely to be blocked on a guest network.

questions.question: A contractor needs to reach only the company's web-based timesheet app, from a personal computer where installing software is not allowed. Which option fits?
choices: A clientless TLS VPN through a web portal
A site-to-site IPsec VPN to the contractor's home
A GRE tunnel from the contractor's PC
An AH-only IPsec tunnel
questions.explanation: Clientless VPNs need only a browser and give access to web applications through a TLS portal. Site-to-site and GRE tunnels need configured gateways, and AH does not encrypt.

questions.question: Which two statements are typical of remote access VPNs rather than site-to-site VPNs? (Choose two.)
choices: The user starts the VPN when needed
A single device is protected by the tunnel
The tunnel is permanently up between two routers
Hosts are unaware that the VPN exists
IPsec between two firewalls is the usual protocol
questions.explanation: Remote access VPNs are on demand and protect one device. Permanent tunnels, host transparency and gateway-to-gateway IPsec describe site-to-site VPNs.

questions.question: With a split-tunnel remote access VPN, a user on hotel Wi-Fi opens a news website. How does that traffic travel?
choices: Through the tunnel to headquarters, then out to the internet
Directly from the hotel network to the internet, outside the tunnel
Through a GRE tunnel to the nearest branch
It is blocked until the VPN disconnects
questions.explanation: Split tunneling sends only traffic for company subnets through the VPN. Other internet traffic goes out directly. A full tunnel would send everything to headquarters first.

questions.question: Two sites are joined by a classic IPsec tunnel, but OSPF will not form a neighbor relationship across it. What is the usual fix?
choices: Switch from ESP to AH
Run GRE over IPsec so the tunnel interface carries OSPF's multicast hellos
Disable Diffie-Hellman
Replace OSPF with static NAT
questions.explanation: Classic IPsec tunnels carry matching unicast traffic only, and OSPF hellos are multicast. A GRE tunnel interface carries them, and IPsec then encrypts the GRE packets.

questions.question: GRE packets are identified in the IP header by which protocol number?
questions.explanation: GRE is IP protocol 47. A firewall between two GRE endpoints must permit protocol 47 (or the IPsec traffic that carries it).

questions.question: R1 and R2 use the tunnel configuration below across the internet, and OSPF works fine. A packet capture on the ISP's network shows the users' traffic in readable form. Why?
questions.code:
interface Tunnel0
 ip address 172.16.0.1 255.255.255.252
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/0
 tunnel destination 128.107.1.1
!
router ospf 1
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
choices: The tunnel needs a /24 mask to enable encryption
OSPF disables encryption on tunnel interfaces
The tunnel source should be a loopback for encryption to work
This is plain GRE, which encrypts nothing; it needs IPsec, such as tunnel protection ipsec profile
questions.explanation: A GRE tunnel only encapsulates. Without IPsec protection the inner packets cross the internet in the clear. Adding tunnel protection (GRE over IPsec) encrypts them.

questions.question: In an SD-WAN or DMVPN design, what is the underlay?
choices: The physical network or internet transport that actually carries the tunneled packets
The set of virtual tunnels and their routing
The encryption algorithm used inside the tunnels
The management VLAN of the WAN routers
questions.explanation: The underlay is the real transport network. The tunnels built on top of it, with their own addressing and routing, form the overlay.

questions.question: In one or two sentences, what does IKE do, and what does ESP do, in an IPsec VPN?
questions.answer: IKE negotiates the tunnel: it authenticates the peers, agrees on algorithms, runs Diffie-Hellman and builds the security associations (UDP 500 or 4500). ESP then protects the actual user packets with encryption, integrity and anti-replay (IP protocol 50).
questions.explanation: Separating negotiation (IKE) from data protection (ESP or AH) is the core structure of IPsec.

questions.question: What is the difference between a tunnel and a secure VPN?
questions.answer: A tunnel is just encapsulation: a packet wrapped inside another packet. It becomes a secure VPN only when protection such as IPsec or TLS adds encryption, integrity and authentication; a plain GRE tunnel has none of these.
questions.explanation: The exam likes to test that GRE is a tunneling protocol without security, which is why it is paired with IPsec.

questions.question: Which kind of encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt, and protects the bulk data in a VPN?
choices: Symmetric encryption, such as AES
Asymmetric encryption, such as RSA
Hashing, such as SHA-256
Digital signatures
questions.explanation: Symmetric ciphers use one shared key and are fast enough for every packet. Asymmetric keys and signatures are used during setup, and a hash cannot be decrypted at all.

questions.question: Match each building block to what it contributes to an IPsec VPN.

pairs.right: Integrity plus proof the sender holds the key
A shared secret that never crosses the network

questions.explanation: Each VPN goal has its own tool: a symmetric cipher hides data, a keyed hash detects changes, signatures with certificates authenticate peers, and Diffie-Hellman agrees on keys.

questions.question: Two IPsec gateways authenticate with certificates instead of a pre-shared key. What allows each gateway to trust the other's certificate?
choices: Both certificates are signed by a certificate authority that each gateway trusts
The certificates contain the pre-shared key
The gateways exchange their private keys during IKE
The certificates are encrypted with AES
questions.explanation: A CA's signature vouches that the public key belongs to the named peer. Private keys never leave their owners, which is the whole point of public key authentication.

questions.question: A company wants a full mesh of site-to-site IPsec tunnels between 6 sites. How many tunnels are needed?
questions.explanation: A full mesh needs n(n - 1)/2 tunnels: 6 x 5 / 2 = 15. Hub-and-spoke would need only 5, at the cost of branch traffic detouring through the hub.

questions.question: A company's sites connect through a carrier's MPLS VPN. An auditor asks whether traffic between the sites is encrypted. What is the accurate answer?
choices: Yes, MPLS VPNs always run IPsec
No, an MPLS VPN keeps customers' traffic separate but does not encrypt it by default
Yes, MPLS labels encrypt the payload
Only routing updates are encrypted
questions.explanation: MPLS VPNs provide separation, not cryptography; the customer trusts the carrier. If policy requires encryption, IPsec has to be added on top.

questions.question: Put the stages of bringing up an IKEv1 site-to-site tunnel in order.
items: Interesting traffic arrives and the router contacts the peer on UDP 500
Phase 1: the peers agree on a policy, run Diffie-Hellman and authenticate each other
The IKE SA is up and protects the rest of the negotiation
Phase 2: the peers agree on a transform set and build two IPsec SAs
User packets flow as ESP, protected by the IPsec SAs
questions.explanation: Traffic triggers IKE, phase 1 builds a protected and authenticated channel, phase 2 negotiates the one-way IPsec SAs inside it, and only then is user data encrypted with ESP.

questions.question: What is an IPsec security association (SA)?
choices: A certificate issued by a CA
The GRE tunnel interface
A list of users allowed to connect
A one-way agreement on keys, algorithms and lifetime for traffic between two peers
questions.explanation: IPsec SAs are unidirectional, so a working tunnel has a pair, each identified by its SPI. The IKE SA from phase 1 is the separate control channel used to negotiate them.

questions.question: Users at the branch say the tunnel to HQ does not work. Based on the output from branch router R1, what is happening?
questions.code:
R1# show crypto ipsec sa
! lines omitted
   local  ident (addr/mask/prot/port): (10.2.2.0/255.255.255.0/0/0)
   remote ident (addr/mask/prot/port): (10.1.1.0/255.255.255.0/0/0)
   current_peer 128.107.1.1 port 500
    #pkts encaps: 512, #pkts encrypt: 512, #pkts digest: 512
    #pkts decaps: 0, #pkts decrypt: 0, #pkts verify: 0
choices: Phase 1 failed, so no SAs exist
R1 is encrypting and sending traffic into the tunnel, but no protected traffic is arriving back from the peer
No traffic matches R1's crypto policy
The tunnel is healthy and simply idle
questions.explanation: Counters on an IPsec SA mean phase 2 succeeded. Encaps rising with decaps at zero means packets leave R1 encrypted but nothing protected returns, so check the HQ side's routing and crypto policy, or a filter dropping ESP toward R1.

questions.question: In ESP tunnel mode, which part of the original packet is encrypted?
choices: Only the TCP or UDP payload
Only the original IP header
The entire original packet, including its IP header
Nothing; tunnel mode only authenticates
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode wraps and encrypts the whole original packet, hiding the private addresses, and adds a new outer header with the gateways' public addresses. Transport mode keeps the original header unencrypted.

questions.question: An edge ACL must let a site-to-site IPsec VPN through, both when the peers see each other directly and when a NAT device sits between them. Which three must it permit between the peers' public addresses? (Choose three.)
choices: UDP 500
UDP 4500
IP protocol 50 (ESP)
IP protocol 47 (GRE)
TCP 1723
questions.explanation: IKE uses UDP 500, ESP is IP protocol 50 without NAT, and with NAT traversal both IKE and ESP move into UDP 4500. In GRE over IPsec, the GRE packets travel inside ESP, so protocol 47 never appears on the outside. TCP 1723 belongs to the old PPTP protocol.

questions.question: Which two protocols can Cisco's remote access VPN client (AnyConnect, now Cisco Secure Client) use to build its tunnel? (Choose two.)
choices: TLS, with DTLS for performance
IPsec with IKEv2
GRE
AH alone
Telnet
questions.explanation: The client normally uses TLS on port 443 (plus DTLS), and it can also use IPsec with IKEv2. GRE and AH provide no encryption, and Telnet is not a VPN protocol.

questions.question: A remote access client builds its tunnel with TLS on TCP 443 and then adds DTLS on UDP 443. Why?
choices: DTLS adds a second layer of encryption on top of TLS
DTLS avoids carrying TCP inside a TCP tunnel, which performs badly for voice and video when packets are lost
DTLS is required to authenticate the user
UDP 443 bypasses the headend's firewall rules
questions.explanation: When a TCP tunnel loses a packet, it retransmits and stalls everything inside it, and the inner TCP sessions react too. DTLS gives the same protection over UDP so real-time traffic is not held up.

questions.question: When a laptop starts a TLS remote access VPN, why does it check the headend's certificate?
choices: To prove the headend is really the company's VPN gateway and not an impostor in the middle
To learn the user's password
To choose the split-tunnel routes
To compress the tunnel traffic
questions.explanation: The certificate, signed by a CA the client trusts, authenticates the gateway. Without that check, an attacker on hotel Wi-Fi could pose as the gateway and collect the user's credentials.

questions.question: How does a carrier's MPLS VPN differ from an IPsec VPN over the internet?
questions.answer: An MPLS VPN keeps each customer's routes and traffic separate inside the provider's network but does not encrypt by default, so the customer trusts the carrier. An IPsec VPN over the internet encrypts and authenticates every packet because nobody on the path is trusted.
questions.explanation: Both are called VPNs, but only one provides cryptographic protection. That is why IPsec is sometimes run on top of MPLS.

questions.question: 300 field sales staff need secure access to internal applications from hotels and customer sites. Which VPN type fits?
choices: A site-to-site IPsec VPN
A remote access VPN with a client on each laptop
GRE tunnels without IPsec
An MPLS VPN to every hotel
questions.explanation: Individual users at changing locations need on-demand tunnels from their own devices. Site-to-site VPNs and MPLS connect fixed sites, and plain GRE provides no security.

questions.question: The branch tunnel to HQ will not come up. Based on the output from branch router R1, what is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
R1# show crypto isakmp sa
IPv4 Crypto ISAKMP SA
dst             src             state          conn-id status
128.107.1.1     64.100.9.9      MM_NO_STATE       1001 ACTIVE (deleted)
choices: The phase 2 transform sets do not match
The tunnel is healthy and waiting for interesting traffic
IKE phase 1 is failing: the policies or pre-shared keys do not match, or UDP 500 is blocked between the peers
ESP is blocked, but IKE works normally
questions.explanation: MM_NO_STATE means main mode (phase 1) never completed, so no IKE SA exists and phase 2 cannot even start. A phase 2 mismatch or blocked ESP would leave phase 1 at QM_IDLE.
